Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A shaggy Highland cow standing in tall golden-green grass on a hillside at sunset, with blue-violet hills and a glint of lake behind its horns

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

18 stepsCanvas: 12 x 16 inFocal point: The cow's face: the gold fringe hanging over its eyes, the pale curved horns and the rounded muzzle Light: A low sun from the upper right, behind the hills: it glows gold in the right of the sky and lights the cow's fringe, the top of its head and its right side from behind.How this lesson was made

Before you start

You are going to paint a shaggy Highland cow standing in tall grass on a hillside at sunset, with soft violet hills and a glint of lake behind it. What makes it sing is the cow's face: the glowing fringe hanging over its eyes, the pale curved horns and the round muzzle. Everything else is there to set that face off.

The light

The low sun sits behind the hills, so the sky glows warm gold and the cow is lit from behind. That light catches the edges of its hair, its fringe and the tips of the grass, while the body facing you stays in warm shadow.

What this painting teaches

  • Horizontal strokes (steps 3, 4, 5, 6). Long, level strokes with the brush held flat, side to side. They build the hills, the lake and the green slope as calm flat bands that seem to stretch away. Keep the far bands lighter and smoother, and keep the water dead level.
  • Thick to thin (steps 12, 13). Press the full width of the brush, then turn onto its edge and lift as you pull, so each mark starts wide and tapers to a point. This is what turns a flat cow shape into long, hanging locks of hair and a glowing rim of light. Leave gaps between the locks so the darker coat shows through.
  • Flicking (steps 16, 17, 18). A quick stroke up from the base of each blade, lifting off as you go, so the mark thins at its tip. It makes the tall grass in three passes, dark first, then olive, then a few bright blades. Load lightly, since too much paint makes flat blobs, and let the dark show between the lighter blades.

The way there

You start with the sky, blending blue into gold and adding a few soft cloud streaks, because it is the farthest thing and the easiest big win. Next come the far hills and the little lake, then the green slope with its dark bushes and a plain meadow, so the whole canvas is covered fast. The sky and hills stop short with a loose, ragged edge where later layers will cover them, so some bare canvas showing early on is expected. Then the cow goes on as one flat shape, gets its shadows and horns, then long gold locks and a bright rim of light. The face comes last on the cow, because it is the focal point. Finally the tall grass is flicked over the cow's legs, so it stands in the grass rather than on it.

This lesson skips about three quarters of a canvas of painting that later layers would cover.

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 The far blue hills; 2 The Highland cow. On your 12 x 16 in canvas the grid lines are 3 in apart across and 4 in apart down. Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The sky 2 steps

This stage lays the sunset sky, the backdrop for everything else.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 5 1/2 in from the top edge.

STEP 1 OF 18 · The sky, 1 of 2

Blend the sunset sky

  • Start: Start in the sky's upper left corner, at the top edge of the canvas, with Soft sky blue, and work across to the right edge.
  • Strokes: Stroke side to side in long bands. Without rinsing, pick up Sunset gold for the band below, then stroke back over the join while wet; add more gold there if a hard line shows.
  • Where the paint sits: The blue stays a thin band along the top edge; the warm yellow fills the rest, brightest toward the right edge, where the low sun is. At the right edge, carry the blue down into a low rounded hump.
  • Leave: The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 3.
  • Stop when: The sky reaches about 4 1/4 in from the top edge for most of its width, and about 6 1/4 in from the top edge at the right edge. Its lower edge is loose and uneven, not a ruled line.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 18 · The sky, 2 of 2

Streak in the gold clouds

  • First: Let the sky dry completely first.
  • Start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 1/2 in from the top edge, with a short streak about 2 1/4 in wide.
  • As in step 1: Sunset gold again, but now the brush is almost dry, and you skim thin streaks over dry paint instead of blending wet bands.
  • Strokes: Dip only the tip in Sunset gold, wipe it nearly dry, and skim lightly side to side with a slight slant, so the marks break up on the canvas texture.
  • Where the paint sits: Make three thin streaks high in the blue band: a short one at the left edge, one near the middle, and a long one about 7 3/4 in wide running to the right edge.
  • Leave: Keep blue showing above, between and below the streaks. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 3.
  • Stop when: Three soft, feathery streaks float in the blue, most of them on the right side of the sky.

Dry brush

Not checked yet

With. flat; old stiff flat (catches the canvas weave best)

Load. Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.

Motion. Light pressure, skimming the surface.

What it leaves. Feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.

Then. Build up in several light passes.

Good for. cloud highlights, grass, wood and fences, highlights on round things

Skim, with almost no paint

  • It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.

The far hills and lake 3 steps

This stage pushes the land far away with soft, flat violet hills and a small glowing lake.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 2 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 5 in from the top edge.

STEP 3 OF 18 · The far hills and lake, 1 of 3

Lay in the far hills

  • First: Let the sky and the cloud streaks dry first.
  • Start: Start at the left edge of the canvas about 2 1/4 in from the top edge, and lay the soft rounded tops of the far hills across to the right edge.
  • Strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right, first along the hilltops, then in level bands lower down.
  • Where the paint sits: The hills are one flat, even color with gentle bumps along the top. Fill solidly down from the hilltops; at the right edge, paint over the low dark hump from step 1.
  • Leave: Keep the warm sky and the cloud streaks clean; don't let the hills creep up into them. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 6.
  • Stop when: A flat band of hills crosses the canvas, its lower edge loose and uneven, about 5 1/4 in from the top edge for most of its width.

STEP 4 OF 18 · The far hills and lake, 2 of 3

Darken the nearer ridges

  • First: Let the hills from step 3 dry first.
  • Start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 2 3/4 in from the top edge, on the band of hills from step 3.
  • As in step 3: The same long, level strokes and the same brush; this time a darker mix, laid as nearer ridges in front of the paler hills.
  • Strokes: Pull long, level strokes to the right, letting the top of the ridge slope gently downward as it goes. Soften the ridge tops; don't make them sharp.
  • Where the paint sits: Lay one long ridge sloping down from the left edge, and a second, lower ridge reaching to the right edge, so the hills read as two ranges, near and far.
  • Leave: Keep the paler peaks of the far hills showing along their whole length. The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 6.
  • Stop when: Darker ridges sit in front of the paler peaks. Their lower edge is loose and uneven, about 5 1/4 in from the top edge for most of the width.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.

Stroke: Horizontal strokes, as in step 3.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 18 · The far hills and lake, 3 of 3

Lay in the glowing lake

  • First: Let the ridges dry first, so the water stays clean.
  • Start: Start at the right edge of the canvas, about 4 3/4 in from the top edge, at the foot of the nearer ridges.
  • As in step 1: The same two colors as the sky, now with the smaller brush, in one small strip of level strokes instead of wide blended bands.
  • Strokes: Pull short, level strokes of Sunset gold from the right edge toward the middle, keeping the brush flat so the water stays dead level.
  • Where the paint sits: The strip is about 1 3/4 in wide and thin. Touch a thin line of Soft sky blue along its top where it meets the ridges.
  • Leave: Keep the darker ridges showing all around the water. Don't tilt it; water always lies flat.
  • Stop when: A small, flat strip of glowing pale water lies at the right edge, the brightest spot below the sky.

The hillside and meadow 3 steps

This stage covers the rest of the canvas with the green slope, its dark bushes and a plain meadow.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge.

STEP 6 OF 18 · The hillside and meadow, 1 of 3

Lay in the green slope

  • First: Let the hills and the lake dry first.
  • Start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, just under the darker ridges from step 4, and work down and to the right.
  • As in step 3: The same long, level strokes with the same brush, but over a much bigger area, all the way down to the bottom edge.
  • Strokes: Pull long side-to-side strokes all the way across, and keep them going down to the bottom edge. Let slight streaks show; they read as grass.
  • Where the paint sits: The slope's top edge rises on the left and runs down toward the lake, covering the loose lower edges of the sky and hills. Fill every bare bit down to the bottom edge.
  • Leave: Keep the lake and the darker ridges showing; stop the green where it meets them.
  • Stop when: A flat green slope covers everything below the hills, to the left, right and bottom edges. No bare canvas is left.

STEP 7 OF 18 · The hillside and meadow, 2 of 3

Dab the dark bushes

  • First: Let the green slope dry first, or the dabs will blur into it.
  • Start: Start near the top of the green hillside, at the left edge of the canvas, with small taps just under the darker ridges.
  • Strokes: Wipe most of the paint off and tap with the tip. Tap more in one spot for a solid bush, fewer taps for a ragged edge.
  • Where the paint sits: Make loose rows of small dark bush patches across the upper slope, from the left edge to the right edge, smaller near the top where they are farther away. Add one or two lone patches lower down.
  • Leave: Keep plenty of the green slope showing between the rows, and leave the lower slope plain.
  • Stop when: Dark patches dot the upper slope in loose, uneven rows. If you get blobs, the brush is too wet: wipe it and tap again.

#6 round
Stroke: Dabbing how to do it, not checked yet

Dabbing also called stippling

Not checked yet

With. round (the tip, for small dots); old stiff brush (for rough patches); a sponge, for soft patches

Load. A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.

Motion. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.

What it leaves. Dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.

Then. Tap a lighter mix on the lit side, leaving the darker taps showing underneath.

Good for. foliage, with an old stiff brush, small dots, with the tip of a round

Tap, don't stroke

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  • A patch went too solid. Tap over it with a lighter or darker mix to break it up.

STEP 8 OF 18 · The hillside and meadow, 3 of 3

Lay in the near meadow

  • First: Let the slope and bushes dry first.
  • Start: Start at the left edge of the canvas, about 8 in from the top edge, on the lower slope below the bushes.
  • As in step 6: Olive green again, but now in short criss-cross X strokes instead of long level ones, smoothing over the dark streaks on the slope.
  • Strokes: Make short criss-cross X strokes, then smooth over them with lighter side-to-side strokes while wet.
  • Where the paint sits: Cover the dark slanting shadow streaks on the lower slope with Olive green, in wide slanting bands all the way down. Work a little Deep green into the lowest bands.
  • Leave: Keep the bushes and the upper slope as they are. Small bits of the slope can show between the bands.
  • Stop when: The lower slope reads as an even, plain meadow, a little darker at the bottom edge, with no grass blades yet.

The cow's shape 3 steps

This stage builds the cow as one big shape, gives it shadows so it looks round, and adds its horns.

Where: Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 2 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge; it's about 8 in wide and 9 in tall.

STEP 9 OF 18 · The cow's shape, 1 of 3

Block in the cow

  • First: Let the meadow dry first.
  • Start: Start with one big oval for the body, its middle about 5 in from the left edge, low on the hillside.
  • Strokes: Add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), bending each one down the way the hair hangs. Add a rounded head piece at the upper right of the body.
  • Where the paint sits: Fill the whole cow flat: the shape is about 7 3/4 in wide and 9 in tall, its top about 4 1/4 in from the top edge. Leave the bottom ragged, as if hair hangs into grass.
  • Leave: Keep the slope clean around the shape; let a small notch of hillside show under the head where the chin tucks in.

STEP 10 OF 18 · The cow's shape, 2 of 3

Shade the cow's shadow side

  • First: Let the cow shape from step 9 dry first.
  • Start: Start just under the top of the cow's head, where the fringe hangs over the face, and work down and to the left.

  • Where the paint sits: Put the dark in long streaks down the body, under the fringe, under the chin and along the bottom, heavier on the shadow side away from the sun.
  • Leave: Keep plenty of the reddish base showing between the dark streaks, especially across the top of the head and the back.

STEP 12 OF 18 · The shaggy coat, 1 of 2

Pull the long gold locks

  • First: Let the shading and horns dry first.
  • Start: Start at the top of the fringe between the horns, and work down over the head, then down the body.
  • Strokes: Press the full width of the brush where each lock starts, then turn onto the edge and lift as you pull down, so each lock tapers to a point.
  • Where the paint sits: Hang the locks over the fringe, the head and the body, in many long tapering strokes. Keep them a bit fewer on the shadowed left side of the body.
  • Leave: Leave gaps so the reddish base and the dark streaks from step 10 show between the locks. Keep the face under the fringe plain.
  • Stop when: The coat reads as long, shaggy locks, light over dark, from fringe to belly. No bright rim yet, and the face is still a plain shape.

Light the rim of the hair

STEP 16 OF 18 · The tall grass, 1 of 3

Flick the dark grass

  • First: Let the cow and the meadow dry first.
  • Start: Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and at the left edge, where the tallest clump is about 5 1/4 in tall.
  • As in step 7: Deep green again, as in the bushes, but now flicked up in tall blades with the fan brush instead of tapped on.
  • Strokes: Load lightly. Set the fan brush at the base of each blade and flick quickly upward, lifting off so each mark thins at the top.
  • Where the paint sits: Make clumps of blades: a tall one at the left edge, several at the bottom of the cow so it stands in grass, more to the right of the cow, and short ones along the bottom edge.
  • Leave: Keep plenty of plain meadow between the clumps; this is only the first, darkest pass.
  • Stop when: Dark blades rise in scattered clumps across the meadow and over the bottom of the cow. Too much paint makes flat blobs.

Flicking

Not checked yet

With. fan (its edge)

Load. A light load. Too much paint makes flat blobs.

Then. Flick a lighter mix over the dark base, fewer as you go up, so the dark shows between the marks.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A long-haired highland cow with wide upturned horns standing in tall grass, backlit by a low golden sun, with layered hazy hills and a strip of water behind and a pale evening sky.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, captions, borders, watermark or unrelated scene: everything in the frame is the painting's scene.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 12 x 16 in, portrait

Done: crop

Left out: a strip of empty sky off the top and a strip of grass off the bottom, each about 1 in at the canvas's scale (11% of the photo in all)

Why: No --canvas, so fit-canvas picked the standard size closest to the photo's 2:3 shape (12 x 16, chosen: default); a crop keeps the whole cow, horn tips to the grass at its legs, so no extend render.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes, small rocks scattered on the green hillside at the left. Textures of hundreds of items: yes, grass blades and seed heads across the bottom third and around the legs (busy outlines them there, 13.1% of the canvas, more than the lavender's 10%), and the cow's single hair strands. Detail inside big shapes: yes, the coat's strands, the fringe's wisps and the sky's small wisps. More parts than max_parts 8: about 8 (sky, clouds, far hills, water, hillside, grass, cow, horns), at the limit.

Changed: Grass and seed heads across the bottom third and round the legs become loose upward strokes of dark green, olive and gold, no single blades; the hillside rocks are removed and the hillside is one slope with a few soft darker patches; the far hills become three flat hazy bands; the water stays one pale shape; the sky becomes a soft pale-blue-to-gold gradient with two or three long cloud streaks; the coat becomes broad long wavy strokes of three or four browns and golds with a golden rim light on the sunlit side; the fringe is a few big curved locks; both horns kept whole with dark tips.

Why: Three of the four answers are yes. busy came down from 13.1% to 0.7%; the three tiles left sit on the fringe and the face's edge, none on the drop list (grass, rocks). The cow, horns, water, hills and light are all there. Kept on the first render.

Fine texture measured: the photo 13.1%, the beginner version 0.7%, the finish 0.9% of the canvas

A backlit Highland cow in tall grass at sunset. What matters is the face: the glowing fringe over the eyes, the pale curved horns and the muzzle, set against soft hazy hills. What's hard is the coat: hundreds of hairs that have to become a few kinds of broad lock and a rim of light, and the grass, which has to become three passes of flicked blades. The lesson is about turning fur and grass into repeated big marks a four-brush kit can make.

Subject: A shaggy Highland cow standing in tall golden-green grass on a hillside at sunset, with blue-violet hills and a glint of lake behind its horns
Focal point: The cow's face: the gold fringe hanging over its eyes, the pale curved horns and the rounded muzzle
Light: A low sun from the upper right, behind the hills: it glows gold in the right of the sky and lights the cow's fringe, the top of its head and its right side from behind.

What it saw, back to front

  1. The sunset sky
  2. The golden cloud streaks
  3. The far blue hills
  4. The lake
  5. The green hillside
  6. The dark bushes on the hillside
  7. The tall meadow grass
  8. The Highland cow
  9. The horns
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint along, back to front is the only technique with version 2 keys (v2_step_range, v2_rules) and the only one with a kit block, which --kit needs. It fits the picture: a sky, layered far hills, a green hillside and tall grass go on back to front, then the cow, its fur passes, horns and rim light, then grass over its legs.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner.yaml)

It has no version 2 keys (v2_step_range, v2_rules) and no kit block, so the v3 run and a kit lesson can't use it.

How the paint recipes were worked out10 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

  • Soft sky blue Delta E 4.3
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part white, a touch of yellow, a touch of burnt sienna

  • Sunset gold Delta E 2.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 6 parts white, 2 parts yellow, 1 part red, 1 part burnt sienna

  • Hazy violet Delta E 1.5
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 6 parts white, 3 parts ultramarine, 1 part burnt sienna

  • Slate violet Delta E 4.4
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part ultramarine, 1 part white, a touch of yellow, a touch of red

  • Olive green Delta E 2.6
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts yellow, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part ultramarine

  • Deep green Delta E 3.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 2 parts yellow, 2 parts ultramarine, 1 part red

  • Rust brown Delta E 3.1
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts burnt sienna, 1 part red, a touch of white

  • Dark umber Delta E 2.8
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 3 parts red, 2 parts ultramarine, a touch of yellow

  • Coat gold Delta E 2.7
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of red, a touch of white

  • Horn cream Delta E 3.2
    in the paintingthe recipe mixed

    Mixer: 1 part burnt sienna, 1 part white, a touch of yellow, a touch of ultramarine

Furthest off: Delta E 4.4. Real tubes vary by brand, so mix, compare with the step picture, and nudge.

Why the steps go in this order18 steps

Back to front, as the technique says: the sky and its clouds first, then the far hills, the nearer ridges and the lake, then the green slope, its bushes and a plain meadow, so the canvas is covered early. The cow goes on as one flat shape, then its shadows and horns, then the locks and the rim of light, and the face last because it is the focal point. The tall grass comes at the very end so it can be flicked over the bottom of the cow, which then stands in the grass rather than on it.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    The farthest thing and the biggest easy win, so it goes first, wet-blended blue into gold in one go.

  2. 2. Streak in the gold clouds

    The clouds sit on the sky, so they wait for it to dry and go on dry-brushed so the blue shows through.

  3. 3. Lay in the far hills

    The far hills are the next layer back to front and need the sky dry so their tops stay clean.

  4. 4. Darken the nearer ridges

    A darker range in front of the far hills gives the distance two steps of depth; it needs the hills dry first.

  5. 5. Lay in the glowing lake

    The lake sits at the foot of the ridges, so it goes on after them, small and flat, with the sky's two paints.

  6. 6. Lay in the green slope

    The green slope is in front of the hills and covers their loose lower edges, so it comes after the whole distance.

  7. 7. Dab the dark bushes

    The bushes sit on the slope and are tapped onto it once it is dry.

  8. 8. Lay in the near meadow

    The near meadow is the base the tall grass and the cow stand in, so it goes on before both.

  9. 9. Block in the cow

    With the background done, the cow goes on as one flat shape that every later cow step builds on.

  10. 10. Shade the cow's shadow side

    Shadow first, over the flat shape, so the light locks later sit on dark and the cow looks round.

  11. 11. Pull the curved horns

    The horns sit on the head and against the hills, so they go on once both are dry, before the locks hang over their bases.

  12. 12. Pull the long gold locks

    The long locks are the coat's main texture and go over the shadows, light over dark.

  13. 13. Light the rim of the hair

    The rim of light is the brightest part of the coat, so it goes on top of the locks, near the end of the cow.

  14. 14. Paint the rounded muzzle

    The face is the focal point, so it comes last on the cow, over the finished coat.

  15. 15. Dot in the nostrils

    The nostrils are the smallest, darkest marks on the face and need the muzzle dry under them.

  16. 16. Flick the dark grass

    The tall grass is the nearest layer; the darkest pass goes first so the lighter blades can sit on it, and it covers the bottom of the cow.

  17. 17. Flick the olive grass

    The middle-value blades go over the dark ones, fewer, so the dark shows between.

  18. 18. Flick the sunlit gold grass

    The brightest, fewest blades go last, as accents where the sun catches the grass.

Filters it tried8 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

Three steps build a shape whose form isn't clear from the picture alone: the cow's whole shape, the hooked horns and the direction the locks hang. Everything else is a flat fill, a gradient, or one repeated mark the words and the Where picture already place. Read against the small pictures, the words match them, with one exception already in review.json: step 1's picture keeps a low dark slate hump at the right edge, and the words carry Soft sky blue into it; step 3 covers it.

  • Step 9: Block in the cow beginner check

    Noticed: An animal appears whole in one step, about 7 3/4 by 9 in, and the words build it from an oval, ( ) pieces and a head.

    Pieces: The body oval first, then a hanging ( ) on each side tucked behind, then the round head at the upper right with the chin notch below it, then a ragged bottom edge where the hair goes into the grass. The pieces follow the words' order.

  • Step 11: Pull the curved horns beginner check

    Noticed: Each horn is a hook: it leaves the head sideways, then bends up to a point, and the left one is longer than the right. One sentence doesn't show the bend.

    Pieces: The head as done, then the left horn as one tapered stroke, then the shorter right one, then the dark tip on each, matching the words' cream stroke then Dark umber on the tip.

  • Step 12: Pull the long gold locks beginner check

    Noticed: Fur following the body: the fringe's locks fan down from the top of the head over the face, while the body's hang straight down with the curve. A beginner would pull them all one way.

    Pieces: The cow as done, then the fringe's locks fanning from one point between the horns, then the body's locks hanging down, fewer on the shadowed left as the words say.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A gradient in level bands; the words give the order (blue, then gold) and where it stops.
  • Step 2: Three thin streaks; the words place each one and the picture shows them.
  • Step 3: One flat band with soft bumps along its top; a fill.
  • Step 4: Two long flat bands sloping down; the words say where each runs.
  • Step 5: A small flat strip at the right edge; the words give its size and place.
  • Step 6: A flat fill to three edges of the canvas.
  • Step 7: One tapped mark repeated in loose rows; a texture.
  • Step 8: A flat fill of criss-cross strokes over the lower slope.
  • Step 10: Dark streaks in the four places the words name, with the card's curved stroke down the body; the picture shows where they go.
  • Step 13: Short strokes along an edge already painted; the words name the edges.
  • Step 14: One small oval, 1 1/2 by 1 in, with the cream along its top; the words give its size, place and order, and the picture shows it.
  • Step 15: Two dots side by side on the muzzle.
  • Step 16: One flicked mark repeated in clumps; the words place the clumps.
  • Step 17: The same flick, fewer blades.
  • Step 18: The same flick, the fewest blades.
What the reviewer caught7 notes

A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Text check: paint Step 12: The paint called Coat gold was measured from the pictures as a deep rust orange (#ad5f28), darker and redder than the gold its name says. (left: a paint's name is in the chain's requests, so renaming it would render part of the chain again; build-steps' note.)
